what_this_is: The Workshop row for the cite-principles-from-captions folder: a script the person's AI runs on the person's own computer to build a corpus from captioned videos, pick the passages worth reading for principles, check every quote against the captions word for word, and merge the principles into one ranked registry with the evidence for each.

payload.label: Keep principles from captioned videos, each backed by a quote checked word for word (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Collect the principles that creators and teachers state or show in their videos, with the exact words and the second they say them, prove every quote is really in the captions, and rank each principle by how many independent channels back it and how well their videos did
payload.description: Works on a folder of YouTube caption files (<id>.en.json3) with their <id>.info.json. corpus: one line per captioned video with its channel, title, views, kind (short or video), the captions as timed lines, and how many times its channel's usual views the video got (the usual is the median from a views table the person gives, or from the folder itself). candidates: the best 40-second windows of each video for what the person wants principles about, scored by their topic words, advice-giving phrases, a matching title and how well the video did, per channel, plus the first 45 seconds of each channel's best videos. find and verify: the second a quote is said at, and a check that every quote in the person's rows is an exact substring of its video's captions (ignoring case, white space and curly apostrophes), telling a wrong quote from a missing caption file and a quote at the wrong second. registry: merges the person's working rows (their own groups, lane names and stage names, passed in as files) into one registry of principles ranked by evidence strength (for each independent channel the best of log2(1 + the video's times-the-usual, capped at 64), halved when the quote only demonstrates the principle), with sources linked to the second, demonstrations, and contradictions linked both ways. What the principles are about, how advice sounds, and how rows group and are named for stages come only from the person's files; the tool holds none. Nothing leaves the computer and no key is needed.

input.description: The folder of caption files (<id>.en.json3) and <id>.info.json on the person's computer, put where {input} is in the command.

output.description: The folder to write corpus.jsonl into, put where {output} is in the command.

output_schema.description: The last line each step prints: {"result": ...}. corpus: {videos, without_captions, corpus}. candidates: {channels: [{channel, videos, passages}], folder}. find: {video, second, found}. verify: {rows, quotes, bad, missing} (exit 1 when bad or missing). registry: {principles, quotes, demonstrations, registry}.

needs: caption files and info files the person already has (for example saved with yt-dlp --write-subs --write-info-json --skip-download)
invoke.say: This runs on the person's own computer, never on Trillion, and installs nothing beyond Python 3. If you can run commands where they are: run `run` with their captions folder in place of {input} and a folder for {output} (add `--views-table FILE.tsv`, columns channel, kind and views, when they have one). Then ask them what the principles should be about, write a terms file {"topic": "word|word", "title": "word|word", "advice": ["phrase", ...]} from their answer, and run `candidates --corpus {output}/corpus.jsonl --terms TERMS --out {output}/candidates`. Read the passages and write their principles as working rows, one JSON per line: id, principle, kind (stated, demonstrated or stated+demonstrated), lanes, sources [{video, t, quote}] with the exact words, demonstrated_in [{video, t, how}], test, do_it, transfer. Run `verify --corpus {output}/corpus.jsonl --rows 'ROWS/*.jsonl'` and fix every BAD, TOFF or MISSING line before going on (`find` gives a quote's second). Then run `registry --corpus ... --rows ... --out principles.jsonl`, with `--merge FILE` ({"groups": [{"ids": [...], "text": ...}], "contradictions": [[id, id, how]]}) and `--lanes FILE` ({"stages": {stage: [lanes]}, "lane_names": {lane: lane}}) when they group or name stages. Tell the person how many principles there are, the strongest by evidence, and any that only one channel backs. If you cannot run commands, give them these steps.

provenance.source: Written for mining many creators' videos for the principles they state and show, with every quote proved against the captions
